title: Argued into the canon
hookLine: the Mishnah records debates over whether Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes belonged (Yadayim 3:5)
carry: a doubt didn't throw a book out

cards: The minutes of the meeting were kept. That's the surprising thing. A library of holy books could have been handed down as if it had always been settled.
Instead, the rabbis of the Mishnah and the Talmud wrote down the arguments. Which books are holy? Does this one belong?
What do we do with a book that seems to contradict itself? And they kept the names of the people who doubted. Earlier on this path, we heard Rabbi Akiva call the Song of Songs the holy of holies.
Today, the other half of that page: the argument he was answering.

teach.h: BOOKS THAT MAKE THE HANDS UNCLEAN.
teach.b: The Mishnah, in tractate Yadayim, uses a strange phrase for scripture: a holy book is one that makes the hands unclean. Then it records a disagreement, almost like a transcript.
One rabbi says the Song of Songs makes the hands unclean, but about Ecclesiastes there's a dispute. Another says the reverse. A third ties the question to the old schools of Shammai and Hillel.
Another reports a ruling that both books do.
Only then comes Akiva's strong answer: no one in Israel, he insists, ever disputed the Song of Songs; if there was a dispute, it was over Ecclesiastes.

The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, adds that the sages wanted to store Ecclesiastes away, because its words seemed to contradict each other, one verse praising what another seems to dismiss. Why didn't they?

teach.h: ITS BEGINNING AND END ARE TORAH.
teach.b: Because its beginning is words of Torah and its end is words of Torah. And the book does end that way, in the King James words: "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man."
So the hard middle was kept because of its frame. These books weren't slipped into the canon quietly.

They were argued into it, out loud, and the record of the argument became part of the tradition too. In this record, a doubt didn't throw a book out; it made the sages look at its first and last lines.

how: Jewish study keeps disagreements on the page: the Mishnah and the Talmud record minority opinions by name alongside the rulings, and students learn the arguments as well as the outcomes.

games.q: you're one of the sages. a book in your library seems to contradict itself. what do you do?
o: hide it away and stop reading it.
keep it, because its beginning and end are Torah.
games.why: the Talmud says the sages wanted to store Ecclesiastes away, but kept it because its beginning and end are words of Torah.

practice: Choose the Song of Songs or Ecclesiastes and hold one line from it, or this one, in the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven."
Ask what would make someone doubt it belongs, then what would make someone fight to keep it. If you pray, give thanks in words from your tradition for the books that were kept.
